title: William Lane Craig vs Peter Millican: Does God Exist?
label: God and skeptical empiricism
motion: Does the evidence from cosmology, fine-tuning, morality, Jesus' resurrection, and religious experience make Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism?
summary: Craig presented five cumulative lines for Christian theism. Millican challenged their causal, probabilistic, moral, historical, and experiential warrants while advancing comparative skepticism. The locked record scores Craig at 67 and Millican at 76.

pro.context: Craig said this while answering Millican's source criticism. He was defending the historical standing of the empty tomb, reported appearances, and the disciples' resurrection belief, not claiming that historian agreement itself establishes a miraculous explanation.

con.text: the world we see just doesn't match up to what you'd expect from a perfect God
con.context: Millican framed evil as comparative empirical evidence. His claim was that observed suffering and morally troubling material fit a perfect deity less well than skepticism, while still requiring further support about the relevant expectations.

sections.title: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator

pro.words: Because the universe began, it requires a transcendent cause whose relation to time, space, matter, and causal regress makes it uncaused, timeless, changeless, spaceless, and immaterial.
pro.critique: Craig’s move has a clear deductive spine: a beginning universe requires a transcendent cause, and the cause is then characterized through the alleged limits of regress, time, space, and matter. That coherence and explicit structure make the move genuinely competent. Its principal limitation is that several crucial warrants are compressed: why every beginning requires a cause, why the relevant regress cannot be infinite, and why creating time entails timeless changelessness. The selected span states these steps more confidently than it establishes them. The live burden is therefore not merely deriving the conclusion from premises, but defending those metaphysical premises against empirical and conceptual alternatives. A final score of 75 fits a strong, intelligible route with one or more material bridges still unresolved.

con.words: Ordinary causal experience concerns rearrangements of existing material, so it does not justify extending the principle that beginnings have causes to creation from nothing.
con.critique: Millican’s reply is strongest where it grants the argument’s validity and isolates the evidential reach of ordinary causal experience. He distinguishes rearrangement of existing material from creation ex nihilo, directly pressuring the premise that whatever begins must have a cause. That accurate reconstruction gives the move clarity and charity. Its principal limitation is coverage: it addresses only one indispensable component of Craig’s larger cosmological route, leaving the beginning premise and the proposed attributes of the cause untouched. A quantum vacuum is not literal nothing. The live burden is to show that the causal generalization extends beyond observed material transformations. A score of 78 appropriately reflects a strong partial answer whose central evidential challenge remains consequential but incomplete.

pro.words: A transcendent cause must be an unembodied mind because the only proposed alternative, an abstract object, cannot cause anything; therefore the universe has a personal creator.
pro.critique: Craig’s personal-cause inference usefully narrows the question after positing a transcendent, nonphysical cause: abstract objects do not cause anything, whereas minds can exercise agency. The move is admirably explicit, easy to audit, and directly oriented toward connecting generic cosmology to a personal creator. Its central defect is the asserted exhaustiveness of the choice between abstract object and unembodied mind. It neither excludes unknown causes nor establishes disembodied mentality. Because that unsupported dichotomy carries nearly the entire inference, the move’s clarity cannot rescue its evidential weakness. The live burden is to justify both the candidate set and the possibility of mentality without a physical substrate. A score of 59 fits a weak but recognizable argument with a clear route and a seriously underdefended central bridge.

con.words: Known minds depend on physical substrates, and a nonphysical cosmic cause need not be an abstract object or mind; it could belong to an unfamiliar causal category.
con.critique: Millican directly diagnoses the vulnerability in Craig’s abstract-object-or-mind dichotomy and gives its consequence: even granting a nonphysical cause, an unfamiliar category could block the inference to personal agency. He adds empirical pressure by noting that known minds depend on physical substrates. This is a responsive and logically clean answer to the selected move. Its limitation is that the appeal to an unknowable kind of cause remains a possibility rather than evidence, and it does not defeat the broader claim that some transcendent cause exists. The live burden is specifically whether Craig has earned the transition from nonphysical causation to mind. A score of 80 belongs in the strong band because the diagnostic defeat succeeds against that transition, despite limited motion-level relevance and incomplete positive support.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning, Alternative Explanations, and Designer Specificity

pro.words: Life-permitting fine-tuning is extraordinarily improbable under chance, is not physically necessary, exhibits an independent pattern, and is therefore best explained by design.
pro.critique: Craig presents a design inference: life-permitting parameters occupy an extremely narrow range, necessity and chance allegedly fail, and an independently specified life pattern favors design. The move’s strongest feature is its organized comparison of rival explanations and its direct contribution to a distinct evidential route. Yet its decisive probability and elimination claims outrun the selected support. The range of physically possible values, their probability distribution, the independence of constants from deeper law, and the adequacy of chance are asserted rather than established. Treating necessity, chance, and design as exhaustive also understates mixed or unknown explanations. The live burden is comparative likelihood, not merely compatibility with design. A score of 71 fits a mixed-to-competent constructive: relevant, but materially underdeveloped warrants and overconfident exclusions.

con.words: Fine-tuning warrants caution because purpose is easily over-detected, cosmic probabilities are uncertain, deeper physics may explain the constants, and multiverse selection could make life-permitting observations unsurprising.
con.critique: Millican answers every indispensable component of the fine-tuning constructive by challenging human purpose detection, current physical completeness, and the exclusion of deeper laws. His strongest feature is disciplined calibration: he first concedes that a genuinely inexplicable selection would invite designer explanation, then argues that present knowledge has not reached that condition. This makes the reply charitable, comprehensive, and responsive. The main limitation is that several alternatives are themselves possibilities rather than quantitatively compared explanations; a multiverse or future theory cannot gain probability simply by being conceivable. Purpose-detection bias is not an alternative explanation. The live burden remains whether design is currently better supported than competitors. A score of 82 fits a strong full answer with broad coverage, sound caution, and bounded evidential gaps.

sections.title: Objective Morality, Divine Character, and the Evidence of Evil

pro.words: Objective moral values are evident in moral experience and require God as their ground; because such values exist, God exists.
pro.critique: Craig’s moral constructive is explicit: objective values and duties would not exist without God; objective morality does exist; therefore God exists. He offers moral experience as evidence and distinguishes objective validity from social acceptance. Those features make the route intelligible and relevant to divine character. Its principal limitation lies in the first premise, which does not exclude secular moral realism, constructivism, or nonnatural moral facts. The move also slides between values and obligations without defending why each requires a divine ground. Because the locked route gives this move no exact bridge contact, its constructive leverage is bounded. The live burden is ontological grounding, not whether people recognize cruelty as wrong. A score of 62 fits a weak-to-mixed case with clarity but an underdefended central warrant.

con.words: Observed evil and purported divine morality do not match expectations for a perfect God, so the world provides comparative empirical evidence favoring skepticism.
con.critique: Millican reframes evil as comparative empirical evidence: a world containing extensive suffering and morally troubling divine commands is less expected under a perfect God, so it favors skepticism. The move’s strength is its clear probabilistic intuition and its direct contact with Craig’s attempt to use evil as support for divine moral grounding. The principal limitation is evidential development. The selected span does not specify the distribution, kinds, or quantities of evil, model the relevant expectations, or engage concrete theodicies; its broad conclusion that very little favors God exceeds what this move alone establishes. The live burden is comparative likelihood under theism and skepticism. A score of 74 fits a competent partial answer: coherent and important, but with the central empirical warrant still compressed.

pro.words: The empty tomb, post-mortem appearances, and disciples' unexpected resurrection belief lack a plausible natural explanation and are best explained by God raising Jesus.
pro.critique: Craig identifies three framed claims—empty tomb, appearances, and the disciples’ resurrection belief—and connects them to a resurrection explanation. The move’s strongest feature is its specificity: it names evidence, cites scholarly support, and offers a route to specifically Christian theism rather than generic design. Its main weakness is the comparative inference. Rejecting a few familiar natural explanations does not establish that no plausible naturalistic account exists. The selected span inadequately compares source dependence, legendary development, psychology, prior probability, or source quality. The assertion that contemporary scholarship universally rejects alternatives is also overbroad. The live burden is whether divine resurrection best explains the claims after serious rival comparison. A score of 67 fits a mixed argument with meaningful evidence and relevance but a materially underwarranted explanatory leap.

con.words: The resurrection accounts are late Christian advocacy documents, lack eyewitness authorship and full independence, and contain chronological and theological discrepancies, weakening their evidential force.
con.critique: Millican supplies source criticism: the accounts are late advocacy texts, not eyewitness reports; Matthew and Luke depend on Mark and another common source; and the narratives contain chronological and theological discrepancies. This gives his reply an evidential core and weakens the independence and reliability of part of Craig’s historical case. Its limitation is incomplete target coverage. Craig’s selected argument invoked appearances, the origin of resurrection belief, and scholarly claims, while Millican largely narrows the case to gospel documents and discrepancies. Treating all four accounts too uniformly reduces representational charity. The live burden is whether these source weaknesses lower the probability of the full three-fact inference. A score of 75 fits a competent partial answer: strong source pressure, but only one major component fully contacted.

sections.title: Religious Experience, Rival Hypotheses, and the Cumulative Burden

pro.words: A sincere seeker can know God apart from argument through immediate personal experience, encountering God as a directly given reality rather than merely adopting an idea.
pro.critique: Craig’s religious-experience move clearly distinguishes immediate acquaintance from public argument and explains why, for the subject, God could be experienced as a given reality rather than inferred as a hypothesis. That makes the claim coherent, intelligible, and relevant to one of his five evidential lines. The principal limitation is the leap from phenomenology to reliable knowledge, especially the universal assurance that sincere seekers will encounter God. The selected span offers no method for distinguishing veridical experience from culturally shaped, psychologically generated, or conflicting religious experiences. It also does not show why private warrant should carry the debate’s comparative public burden. The live issue is reliability and discrimination, not sincerity or vividness. A score of 61 fits a weak-to-mixed constructive: understandable and topical, but substantially underwarranted.

con.words: The specific Christian God competes with thousands of incompatible religious hypotheses, so without an overwhelmingly strong comparative case, disbelief or at least agnosticism is rational.
con.critique: Millican’s cumulative-burden move emphasizes the specificity of the Christian hypothesis and the existence of many incompatible religious alternatives. He grants prior probability to disembodied mentality before asking how that probability should be distributed. This is fair-minded, motion-level, and relevant to whether Christian theism is more reasonable than skepticism. Its main defect is probabilistic. The allocation among thousands of religions is not justified by a partition or evidence model, and the move from an insufficient case to positive atheism is faster than the move to agnosticism. Counting hypotheses does not determine their priors. The live burden is a comparative posterior judgment across the evidence. A score of 75 fits a strong constructive in relevance and framing, moderated by underdeveloped probability warrants and an overextended default conclusion.

strengths: Landed: Craig gave the cosmological route an explicit deductive structure and later answered Millican's Borde-Guth-Vilenkin objections directly, earning an 80 on that reply.
Landed: His fine-tuning case clearly identified necessity, chance, and design as competitors and remained a relevant independent evidential line despite unresolved probability warrants.
Landed: The resurrection case named three historical claims and supplied scholarly support rather than relying solely on confessional assertion.
Landed: His concession that the presented arguments establish enormous rather than infinite power was exceptionally well calibrated and earned 75.

blunders.text: Whiffed: The inference from a nonphysical cause to an unembodied mind depended on an unsupported exhaustive dichotomy, leaving the personal-creator bridge at 59.

Whiffed: The religious-experience and evil replies relied on speculative assurances about sincere seekers, available evidence, and salvation-maximizing suffering, contributing to weak section results.

strengths: Landed: Millican granted the Kalam argument's validity before isolating the limited evidential basis for extending ordinary causation to creation ex nihilo.

Landed: His fine-tuning reply contacted purpose detection, probability uncertainty, deeper physics, and multiverse selection while expressly conceding when design would become evidentially attractive.
Landed: He diagnosed the abstract-object-or-mind dichotomy and explained why an unfamiliar nonphysical cause would defeat the personal-mind inference.
Landed: His source criticism identified dependence and discrepancies in the resurrection narratives, while his evil argument supplied direct comparative pressure against divine perfection.

blunders.text: Whiffed: The allocation of prior probability across thousands of religions was not formally defended, and the transition from insufficient evidence to atheism moved faster than the transition to agnosticism.
Whiffed: His resurrection criticism concentrated on gospel documents and did not fully engage the appearances, disciples' belief, or broader historical support in Craig's selected case.

finalArgument.thesis: Christian theism can be defended most responsibly as a comparative cumulative explanation whose several evidential lines provide modest, partly independent support rather than individually decisive demonstrations.
premises: If the universe has a finite past, a transcendent causal explanation becomes a live option, although further argument is required to identify that explanation as personal.
Fine-tuning supports design only to the extent that a defensible probability measure and comparative model make life-permitting conditions less expected under relevant natural alternatives.
A moral argument should distinguish the existence, authority, and epistemic accessibility of moral truths and explain separately why divine character best grounds each relevant feature.
The resurrection inference gains force only after source dependence, psychological alternatives, prior probability, and the explanatory scope of competing hypotheses are compared explicitly.
Religious experience may provide defeasible personal justification when accompanied by cross-cultural checks, openness to error, and independent evidence, but it cannot bear the public case alone.
finalArgument.conclusion: If these qualified lines retain support after explicit rival comparison and their evidential dependencies are controlled, they can jointly make Christian theism somewhat more reasonable without making disbelief irrational.

newArguments.title: Dependence-adjusted convergence
newArguments.text: A stronger cumulative case would model the evidential lines as a dependency graph rather than simply counting them. Cosmological and fine-tuning evidence may overlap through shared physical assumptions, while resurrection and religious-experience claims may overlap through prior theistic commitments. Moral evidence could be more independent. If each line still contributes a positive likelihood ratio after those dependencies are discounted, their convergence would be evidentially meaningful without requiring any single argument to be decisive.

newArguments.title: Publicly constrained religious experience
newArguments.text: Religious experience could be defended by analogy with other defeasible perceptual beliefs only under explicit constraints: the experience should cohere over time, avoid contradiction with well-supported public facts, remain open to psychological explanation, and gain weight from independent evidence. Conflicting traditions would reduce confidence rather than automatically nullify every experience. This approach preserves limited first-person warrant while conceding that private experience alone cannot establish the specifically Christian hypothesis for an external audience.

finalArgument.thesis: Skeptical atheism is best defended as the comparative judgment that the specific Christian God hypothesis receives insufficient net support once uncertainty, alternative explanations, divine hiddenness, and evil are evaluated together.
premises: Ordinary causal evidence does not by itself establish causation outside spacetime, and a nonphysical first cause would not without further argument identify a personal mind.
Fine-tuning cannot strongly favor the Christian God until probability measures, natural alternatives, and the designer's expected aims are specified rather than treated as open placeholders.
Secular moral realism remains a live alternative unless theism explains moral facts, obligations, and knowledge better rather than merely asserting that naturalism lacks a foundation.

Historical resurrection claims require assessment against source dependence, psychological mechanisms, legendary development, base rates, and alternative explanations before a miracle can become the preferred account.
Apparently gratuitous suffering and sincere nonbelief count against a perfectly good, relationship-seeking God when those observations are more expected under skeptical alternatives.
finalArgument.conclusion: Unless the Christian hypothesis outperforms these natural and skeptical alternatives across the complete evidence, withholding belief is justified, while positive atheism should remain proportionate to the strength of the contrary evidence.

newArguments.title: Specificity penalty without hypothesis counting
newArguments.text: The skeptical case need not divide probability mechanically among thousands of religions. It can instead ask whether each evidential line discriminates the Christian God from generic intelligence, finite designers, morally neutral creators, deism, and naturalistic models. Evidence that fits many rivals has a weak likelihood ratio for Christianity even if it supports some broader supernatural category. This supplies a principled specificity penalty without assuming that every named religion receives an equal prior probability.

newArguments.title: Joint evidence from suffering and hiddenness
newArguments.text: Suffering and sincere nonbelief can be evaluated jointly. A perfectly good God seeking freely chosen relationship might permit some hardship and ambiguity, but the hypothesis should still predict a discernible connection between openness, available evidence, moral growth, and access to relationship. If severe suffering appears poorly connected to those goods while diligent seekers remain unconvinced, the combined observation creates stronger comparative pressure than either evil or hiddenness considered alone.
